prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose, with poetry as its ground, in which memory, the body and dream are built into a cosmological imaginative world.

statement.case_for: My first-place view of Cărtărescu holds after reading the openings. On the common criteria he scores strongly on distinctiveness of voice, formal ambition, imaginative and intellectual depth, and the coherence of a long project. Public knowledge of Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid, together with the poetry and essays named in the entry, points to one imaginative world that is extended across decades rather than repeated. The case rests on the form and language of that world, and not on national or symbolic significance. A single-writer citation is clean: one author, one prize part, and fiction as the core with poetry as context.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that much of the case depends on Romanian prose texture, long-sentence control and wordplay, which I cannot assess directly and which translation may flatten. Very long, self-referential novels may also be uneven across their length, and their breadth of significance beyond readers of ambitious fiction is uncertain. The shared first place across all six openings is not literary evidence, and I would want the committee to test the case against these doubts. This is a judgment from public knowledge and reception, not from independent verification of the texts.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Cărtărescu first because the case for a singular voice and idiom seems strongest there, and he places Anne Carson second for formal reinvention through dialogue with antiquity. He also ranks Alexis Wright last of his eight because the major novels are few.
responses.response: I agree that voice and idiom are the strongest grounds for Cărtărescu, and I would keep the discussion on them rather than on the fact that we ranked him alike. I would qualify Olsson's reading of Wright. A small number of major novels can still carry sustained achievement if their scale, language and formal reinvention are large, and Carpentaria and The Swan Book are very ambitious in just those respects. His point does bear on how confident we can be about breadth over time, which is why I keep her as an alternative and not as my first choice.

responses.point: Sward ranks Cărtărescu first but notes that the very long, self-referential novels may limit breadth of significance. She ranks Yan Lianke second for a formally inventive grotesque and mythic fiction, supported by his own poetics of mythorealism.
responses.response: Sward's breadth concern is fair, and I do not think it can be dismissed. My answer is that the project's breadth comes from joining the intimate (body, memory, dream) to the encyclopedic, and from its reach across poetry and prose, and not from a variety of subject matter. I did not rank Yan Lianke in my opening eight, mainly because I cannot judge his Chinese prose through translation. Sward's argument that the case rests on narrative form, not on political symbolism, is the right standard. I would like the committee to look at how that form works across the large body of work before I could move him above my alternatives.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for the scale and linguistic density of his architecture, and Murnane second for restraint and self-scrutiny. She ranks Carson sixth because it is unclear whether her later work consolidates or only repeats her early breakthroughs.
responses.response: I share Mattson's worry that the Romanian long-sentence control, which is central to the case, may be flattened in translation. On Murnane I partly agree: I ranked him fourth for the rigor and singularity of the project, but his narrow range makes the claim to wide significance harder than for the larger projects. On Carson I would put the question differently. The repeated returns to classical material and to the book as object may be a developing method and not a restatement. Still, Mattson is right that this needs to be shown across volumes and not assumed from Autobiography of Red and Nox.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first for the coherence and scale of the oeuvre. She asks of Carson whether the achievement is sustained over many volumes or concentrated in a few landmark books, and how a formally radical, ironic body of work fits the will's reference to an idealistic tendency.
responses.response: Carlberg's question about Carson is the one that most affects my third-ranked candidate. I find the voice and intellectual depth compelling, but I share her uncertainty about concentration in a few books and about the weight of the translations and classical scholarship, which sit at the edge of the creative oeuvre. I would answer the point about the will by asking what the work attempts, which is a renewal of the ancient–modern relationship, and not by judging its irony alone. I do not think that settles it, and it is a reason I keep Carson as an alternative and not as my choice.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Adonis second, citing a major reshaping of Arabic poetic language. He calls timing delicate because of Adonis's age.
responses.response: I ranked Adonis eighth, and that placement reflects my limits more than a low estimate of his achievement. Poetry in translation loses the prosody and the resonance of inherited forms, which are central to his case, so I am the wrong judge of how large the formal achievement is. I take Sem-Sandberg's argument for it seriously. I would object, however, to letting his age enter as a consideration: the question for the committee is the literary achievement of the oeuvre, and timing should not decide it. I would welcome the view of members who can judge the Arabic more closely.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's effect depends on Romanian sentence rhythm and wordplay that translations may not carry; my judgment rests on public knowledge of the works and their reception, not on independent reading.
Whether the late, very long novels sustain their quality across their full length, and how well the poetry and early work are covered in translation.
How the committee should weigh breadth of significance against singularity of voice and scale when comparing a large single project with several differently shaped oeuvres.
The corpus size and sustained quality for Wright (a smaller number of major novels) and for Carson (hybrid works, translations and book-object forms).
I cannot assess Yan Lianke's Chinese prose or Adonis's Arabic poetics through translation, and the discussion of both rests on colleagues' public-knowledge summaries.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own practice with myth, fairy tale and ekphrasis, and my work on Selma Lagerlöf, are context only and do not indicate a connection to any shortlisted writer.
